text: About 43 percent (between 25 and 66) that a borehole here yields enough for a handpump through the dry season. Provisional prior.
Success means a yield of at least 1 m3/h (0.28 L/s) at the dry-season water level, the handpump design rate in the configuration.

The prior is 63 percent (between 43 and 81), for the BGS class CSF-L/M on the USGS unit pCm: BGS Low to Moderate productivity, read as the span from Low (0.1 L/s) to Moderate (5 L/s) as the guide's other spanning codes are (O Dochartaigh 2021, Tables 1 and 3). No cited source separates the Precambrian unit within the class, so the class's yields apply. Read as the quartiles of a lognormal spread, 0.1 and 5 L/s put 63 percent of boreholes at or above 0.28 L/s. It is held as firmly as 10 boreholes would hold it, and has not been calibrated against boreholes drilled here.

text: The bill of quantities is the contract document: it prices one borehole at the likely rate of every item, and it is what a contractor prices and is paid against. The distribution is the planning figure: what a borehole is likely to cost once the spread of every rate, the drilling depth and the chance of a dry hole are allowed for. Budget from the planning figure; contract on the bill of quantities.
A completed borehole costs US$ 8,332 at P50 and US$ 8,523 at P80, over 300 sampled boreholes. The bill of quantities prices it at US$ 7,829, at or above the cost of 1 percent of them.

Each figure is the contract price with any VAT, before contingency, worked out from the direct cost with the same overheads (15 percent) and margin (20 percent) as the bill of quantities; the spread takes the place of the contingency. With its 10 percent contingency the planning budget, US$ 8,612, covers 88 percent of the sampled boreholes.

Allowing for dry holes at the chance of a working borehole at VES 1, about 60 percent, the expected cost per working borehole is US$ 10,661: the mean completed borehole, and the mean dry attempt, US$ 3,504, for each of the dry attempts expected before a working one. A dry attempt pays for siting, set-up and drilling, as in the programme estimate, but not the journey from the base, which the rig has made already.
The range of models has not been sampled, so the depth is held at 40 m and its spread is left out; sample the range of models to draw the depth from it.

Basis: each unit rate is drawn from a triangle between its minimum, likely and maximum in borehole_cost_items.csv. The rates in one group of borehole_cost_spread.yaml share a cause and are drawn together; the groups are drawn independently, so a cause shared across groups, such as the exchange rate, is spread less than it should be. The minimum and maximum are provisional choices, each with its reason in borehole_cost_spread.yaml, and none has a recorded source. Seed 1.

text: A second sounding beside productive is worth up to US$ 26 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It costs more than it is worth to this decision.

Without it, drilling at productive first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 51 percent, against 30 at point productive. Drilling at productive, and going to point productive if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 14,121 for a working borehole; going to point productive straight away, US$ 16,689.

The choice changes, to going to point productive, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 0.40, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 4 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 14,121 to US$ 14,095.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at productive would work would be worth US$ 1,712 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.

The range of models has not been sampled at productive, so a second sounding is read, as this one was, for its water-zone resistivity alone, and is worth what a profiling line is; sample the range to count its depth to basement too.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

values.summary: A second sounding beside clayey is worth up to US$ 151 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It is worth more than it costs.
text: A second sounding beside clayey is worth up to US$ 151 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It is worth more than it costs.

Without it, going to point resistive is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 41 percent, against 38 at clayey. Going there straight away is expected to cost US$ 13,331 for a working borehole; drilling at clayey first, and going to point resistive if it is dry, US$ 13,596.

The choice changes, to drilling at clayey, on the readings whose factors multiply to more than 1.14, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 34 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 13,331 to US$ 13,180.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at clayey would work would be worth US$ 1,906 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (0.6). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: A profiling line through dry cannot change this decision: nothing it could read moves the chance at dry past the alternative's, so it is worth nothing to it. It costs about US$ 150.

Without it, going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 43 percent, against 25 at dry. Going there straight away is expected to cost US$ 13,007 for a working borehole; drilling at dry first, and going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground if it is dry, US$ 14,449.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at dry would work would be worth US$ 1,180 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

Without it, going to point unknown_fit is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 98 percent, against 78 at unknown_fit. values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: A second sounding beside rounded is worth up to US$ 38 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It costs more than it is worth to this decision.

Without it, going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 43 percent, against 30 at rounded. Going there straight away is expected to cost US$ 13,007 for a working borehole; drilling at rounded first, and going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground if it is dry, US$ 14,093.

The choice changes, to drilling at rounded, on the readings whose factors multiply to more than 1.79, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 17 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 13,007 to US$ 12,968.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at rounded would work would be worth US$ 1,383 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

Drilling at productive, and going to point productive if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 10,552 for a working borehole; going to point productive straight away, US$ 10,552.

The choice changes, to going to point productive, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 1.00, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 46 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 10,552 to US$ 10,317.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at productive would work would be worth US$ 1,363 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

facies.ca_hco3: The water is a Ca-HCO3 type (Ca 65%, Mg 22%, Na+K 13%; HCO3 76%, Cl 15%, SO4 9%, in milliequivalent percent): a fresh, recently recharged water of the kind weathering of silicate rock gives; typical of shallow basement groundwater.
facies.na_hco3: The water is a Na+K-HCO3 type (Ca 13%, Mg 7%, Na+K 80%; HCO3 75%, Cl 15%, SO4 10%, in milliequivalent percent): a bicarbonate water in which sodium and potassium have replaced calcium, which points to longer contact with the rock or to ion exchange in a clayey weathered zone.
facies.mixed_hco3: The water is a mixed-cation-HCO3 type (Ca 40%, Mg 25%, Na+K 35%; HCO3 63%, Cl 30%, SO4 7%, in milliequivalent percent): a bicarbonate water with no single dominant cation, in which calcium and magnesium together still outweigh sodium and potassium; a fresh water of the kind weathering of silicate rock gives, with the sodium share pointing to feldspar weathering or some ion exchange along the flow path.
facies.na_cl: The water is a Na+K-Cl type (Ca 10%, Mg 10%, Na+K 80%; HCO3 14%, Cl 80%, SO4 6%, in milliequivalent percent): a sodium chloride water, which in this setting points to salinity from the coast, an estuary or evaporation rather than to rock weathering.
facies.ca_cl: The water is a Ca-Cl type (Ca 68%, Mg 11%, Na+K 20%; HCO3 23%, Cl 68%, SO4 9%, in milliequivalent percent): a calcium chloride water, which is unusual in fresh basement groundwater; it can point to saline water exchanging with the aquifer or to pollution, and is worth checking against the sample's provenance.
facies.mixed_cl: The water is a mixed-cation-Cl type (Ca 37%, Mg 29%, Na+K 34%; HCO3 19%, Cl 71%, SO4 10%, in milliequivalent percent): a chloride water with no single dominant cation, which points to salinity or pollution mixed into the groundwater rather than to rock weathering alone.
facies.so4: The water is a Ca-SO4 type (Ca 50%, Mg 25%, Na+K 25%; HCO3 25%, Cl 12%, SO4 62%, in milliequivalent percent): a sulfate water, which is unusual in basement ground and worth checking against the sample's provenance.
facies.ca_mixed_anion: The water is a Ca-mixed-anion type (Ca 75%, Mg 12%, Na+K 12%; HCO3 38%, Cl 32%, SO4 30%, in milliequivalent percent): a water with no single dominant anion, of mixed origin or in transition between types.
facies.mixed: The water is a mixed-cation-mixed-anion type (Ca 38%, Mg 30%, Na+K 33%; HCO3 38%, Cl 32%, SO4 30%, in milliequivalent percent): a mixed water with no single dominant ion pair.

Water quality sampling and laboratory analysis.

The recovery line does not pass through the origin: it meets t/t' = 1 at 20.0 m of residual drawdown (60% of the 33.4 m the recovery started from), where Theis recovery requires zero. Steps 2 and 3 open at or before the minute the step before each ended, so their times are read as counted from the start of each step rather than from the start of the test: each step's own last reading is taken as its length, and the steps pumped for 158 minutes in all, not the 60 minutes the latest reading gives. Check the times on the sheet.
The recovery is read against an equivalent pumping time of 112 minutes at the last rate of 3 m3/h (the volume pumped over all the steps at that rate), not the 158 minutes the test ran.
Step 1 ends at -4.32 m drawdown, at or above the static level, so it is left out of the Hantush-Bierschenk fit; check the static level and the datum for that step.

confidence_reasons: each step ran for 50 minutes, below the 60 needed to see late-time behaviour, so the yield is extrapolated 4.0 log cycles of time
each step lies inside the 80-minute casing-storage period, so its drawdown is the borehole emptying rather than the aquifer responding
no transmissivity method fitted to standard and the Cooper-Jacob value is adopted as the best available
short_steps.pump_depth_basis: Pump intake at 47 m: the static level 10.0 m plus the 2 m dry-season reserve, the 31.5 m of drawdown the long-term yield is projected to use and 3 m of submergence; the test itself drew the level to 34.5 m at 3 m3/h. The safety factor is kept on the rate, not spent on raising the pump.
short_steps.envelope_basis: Range over transmissivity 1.7-3.7 m2/day, storativity 0.0001-0.01, effective radius 0.075-0.15 m and a dry-season decline of 1-4 m. Design to the lower figure where the supply must not fail in a dry year.
flags: Each step ran for 50 minutes, below the 60 minutes needed to see late-time behaviour; the yield is extrapolated 4.0 log cycles of time to the 365-day design period and should be treated as indicative.

With a 5 inch casing and a specific capacity of 0.13 m3/h per m, casing storage controls the drawdown for the first 80 minutes (Schafer's rule); each step pumped for 50 minutes, entirely inside it. The Cooper-Jacob and Theis fits see the borehole emptying rather than the aquifer. No fit outside that period can be adopted, so the Cooper-Jacob value is adopted only as the best available and the Theis value is reported but not adopted.

No method fitted to standard (Cooper-Jacob 2.50 m2/day, its fitted window 5-50 minutes lies inside the 80-minute casing-storage period; Theis curve fit 2.50 m2/day, each 50-minute step lies inside the 80-minute casing-storage period). The Cooper-Jacob value of 2.50 m2/day is adopted as the best available, so the yield rests on a fit that does not meet it.

positions.note: The site is at T, Western Area, 8.37587 N, 13.10237 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Holocene (Qe). Bullom Group (Q, Tb), Miocene to Recent. Sands, clays, clayey sands and lignite over the coastal lowland; alluvium along the drainage. Intergranular, generally the best yields available without deep drilling. Shallow water tables mean the protective cover is thin, so siting must keep clear of latrines and surface drainage. The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas classes the aquifer here as Unconsolidated intergranular aquifer - moderate to high productivity (tertiary-quaternary unconsolidated sediments). Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

positions.note: The site is at T, Port Loko district, 8.40000 N, 13.18000 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Paleozoic Igneous (Pi). Freetown Layered Complex (Jf), Jurassic (about 193 Ma). Layered gabbro, norite and anorthosite; a basic to ultrabasic intrusion forming the Freetown peninsula hills. Massive and crystalline, with negligible primary porosity. Groundwater is confined to the weathered mantle and to fracture and joint sets; yields are modest and highly site-dependent, so the fracture target is the whole of the siting problem. The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas classes the aquifer here as Igneous intrusive aquifer - low productivity (igneous intrusive). Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

positions.note: The site is at T, Kono district, 9.39200 N, 10.39600 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Mesozoic Igneous (Mi). Dolerite (Jd), Jurassic. Dolerite, intruded as dykes and sheets cutting the basement. A dyke is usually a barrier rather than an aquifer, but its margins are commonly fractured and its contact with the country rock can concentrate flow. The dyke itself is the wrong target; the contact beside it may be the right one. Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

positions.note: The site is at T, Karene district, 9.49670 N, 12.24050 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Precambrian (pCm). Precambrian basement, chiefly Leonean granite (LG, Lg, PLg, LM, Er, Lkm, Lkt), Archaean to Palaeoproterozoic. Crystalline basement, but not one rock. Cross-tabbed against the bundled BGS hydrogeology on a 1.4 km national grid, 87% of this class is basement aquifer and 12% is consolidated sedimentary with fracture flow - the Rokel River Group belt through Port Loko, Kambia, Moyamba and Tonkolili. On the 2017 map the basement part is chiefly Leonean granite (LG), with Liberian granite (Lg), migmatitic gneiss (PLg, LM), the Magbele and Tapr formations (Lkm, Lkt) and a mylonite zone. Mostly the crystalline basement aquifer this toolkit is built for: no primary porosity, water in the weathered and fractured zone above fresh rock, yield following regolith thickness and the fracture set at the weathered-fresh contact. But this class is not one rock, and where it covers the Rokel River metasediments the aquifer is fracture flow in indurated beds with shales acting as aquicludes - a different target. Read the aquifer map beside it: the BGS layer separates the two where this one does not. The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas classes the aquifer here as Basement aquifer - low productivity (precambrian craton). Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

unplaced_geology.geology: The project area lies within the Freetown Basic Complex. The Freetown Complex is a layered gabbroic anorthosite intrusion emplaced against gneisses and schists of the Kasila Group, and it forms part of the Peninsula and Banana Islands. It is thought to have been formed by multiple injections of magma that occurred intermittently. Groundwater potential within the Freetown Basic Complex is found within weathered and fractured zones of these igneous (crystalline) rocks. Groundwater quality and quantity can be high if the borehole is properly located through appropriate hydrogeological and geophysical investigations.

The project area lies within the crystalline basement terrain of Sierra Leone, where groundwater occurs mainly within the weathered overburden (regolith) and in fractured zones of the underlying bedrock. The weathered zone develops on granites, gneisses and related rocks, and its thickness and degree of fracturing control the groundwater potential. Groundwater quality and quantity can be favourable where the borehole position is properly located through appropriate hydrogeological and geophysical investigations.

sheets.title: Pumping test field sheet: borehole KTL-01
sheets.code: Sheet code GWT-FK/1|pumping|Rokel 2026|KTL-01. Scan it, or type it in, to match this sheet to its project and borehole.
notes: Casing storage: if the transmissivity is as low as 1 m2/day, the water levels of the first 307 minutes may show the 5 inch casing, with its 1.25 inch riser, emptying rather than the aquifer (31 minutes at 10 m2/day).
Constant discharge test: do not stop the pump before 307 minutes, the longer of that time and the shortest constant test the analysis accepts, 240 minutes.
Step test: run every step for at least 60 minutes, and the first for at least 307 minutes, since the drawdown is fitted on the first step.
A shorter test is safe only once the measured drawdown shows a shorter casing-storage time. The pumping test co-pilot or the office works that out from the discharge and the drawdown.
Read the water level at each minute in the Time column, counted from the moment the pump starts. After 120 minutes, read every 30 minutes.
When the pump stops, start the clock again from zero and read the recovery at the same minutes.
sheets.discharge_note: Record the discharge of every step. Time a bucket of known volume three times; the rate in m3/h is 3.6 times the litres divided by the mean seconds. A step with no discharge is written as Not measured, with the reason.
sheets.transcribe: The tables below have the columns of the standard pumping test workbook, so a filled sheet is typed into it cell for cell.

cards.title: Quick card: VES Schlumberger spacings
lines: A sounding reaches a depth of about 0.5 times its largest AB/2. Peg down the table until the depth reached is at least the target depth, and stop there.
AB is always at least 5 times MN, and MN is widened before AB passes 20 times it. Where MN changes, read the same AB/2 again with the new MN, and keep both readings.

cards.title: Quick card: disinfecting the borehole with chlorine
lines: Shock dose of 20 mg of chlorine per litre: add 1 litre of 0.2 percent chlorine solution for every 100 litres of water standing in the well, and do not pump for at least 4 hours.
A 0.2 percent solution holds 2 g of chlorine per litre: dissolve about 3.1 g of 65 percent HTH powder in each litre of water.
Water in the well, in litres, is 0.785 times the square of the casing inner diameter in mm, times the water column in m, divided by 1,000.

tables.caption: Litres of 0.2 percent solution (L) and grams of 65 percent HTH (g), by water column and casing inner diameter.

notes: Basis: the toolkit's supervision checklist (borehole disinfected with chlorine at 20 mg per litre, after Adekile, 2014) and its dose calculator, which follows WHO. Where the programme's own disinfection procedure sets a different dose, it takes precedence.

references: Adekile, D. (2014). Supervising Water Well Drilling: a Guide for Supervisors. RWSN/Skat, St Gallen.
